dailyBrief.text: Big diplomatic day overnight: U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff met President Putin in St. Petersburg carrying the Oslo peace ideas for Ukraine — and Russia freed detained American schoolteacher Stephen Hubbard as the talks began — while Vice President Vance was in Israel trying to hold the fragile Gaza ceasefire together. Washington is consumed by the shutdown's 22nd day — another funding vote failed, and Thanksgiving travel worries are growing. Solon woke up clear and cold at 38°, but it's a sunny, dry day ahead with a high near 66°. No Cleveland teams played last night, so today is the calm before a fun stretch: the Cavs open tomorrow night in Philadelphia, trunk-or-treat is Thursday evening in Solon, and a certain former president has a Solon stop on his Saturday schedule.

weekBrief.text: A dry, golden fall week in Solon: mostly sunny skies, highs in the mid-60s warming to 71–72° Sunday and Monday, and chilly nights in the upper 30s to upper 40s — perfect trunk-or-treat weather for Thursday evening in Solon and Saturday's Trick-or-Treat Trail at the Community Center. It's a huge Cleveland sports week at home: the Cavs play their home opener Saturday against Brooklyn, then host Minnesota Monday and Washington Wednesday, while the first-place Browns are on the road at Tennessee Sunday and Ohio State rests on its bye before Halloween night at USC. Don't miss Heinen's clam bake Friday in Chagrin Falls or the farmers market season finale there Sunday. Grocery play of the week: Miles' jumbo eggs are $1.00 a dozen and Giant Eagle's pork shoulder is $1.99/lb — and with baby watch very much on, it's a good week to finish a few more nursery checklist items together.

Putin hosts Witkoff in St. Petersburg for Ukraine peace talks — and Russia frees a detained American
items.summary:
President Vladimir Putin hosted U.S. special envoy Steve Witkoff in St. Petersburg on Wednesday, their ninth in-person meeting, to review the new peace ideas Witkoff brought from Tuesday's talks in Oslo with President Zelenskiy and European leaders. The meeting, at a grand imperial palace, opened with a goodwill gesture: Russia released Stephen Hubbard, a 74-year-old retired American schoolteacher held since 2022.

Hubbard, originally from Michigan, had been serving a nearly seven-year sentence after a closed-door trial convicted him of mercenary activity — charges his lawyer says he denied — and he was the only American prisoner in Russia formally designated by Washington as wrongfully detained. Putin said Hubbard had been freed and was at St. Petersburg's Pulkovo airport. In the talks, Witkoff said there was a basis for a ceasefire and raised resuming three-way talks among Russia, the U.S. and Ukraine, while Putin thanked President Trump for his efforts and floated meeting him in China.

The diplomacy comes as U.S.–Ukraine ties have frayed over a recent U.S.–Russia diesel export deal and Ukrainian complaints about disrupted intelligence sharing and its Starshield satellite link — issues Zelenskiy said the Oslo meeting resolved. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, traveling in India, called the Oslo session positive and said Witkoff carried its results to the Russian side.

Watch for any Kremlin or White House readout on ceasefire terms. Movement toward three-way talks would be real progress; another round of statements without dates would suggest the gap is still wide.

items.title: Vance works to hold a fragile Gaza ceasefire together in Israel
items.summary:
Vice President JD Vance was in Israel on Wednesday trying to keep a fragile Gaza ceasefire from unraveling, meeting Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu as U.S. envoys pressed both sides to stick to the deal. The truce has been tested by fresh violence and by a slow, painful process around hostages and remains.

Israel has received the remains of additional hostages through the Red Cross, while disputes continue over aid, Hamas disarmament and who governs Gaza next. President Trump has warned Hamas publicly even as his team argues the ceasefire framework is still the best path to ending the war.

The stakes go well beyond one truce. If the ceasefire holds, it opens space for reconstruction and a political settlement; if it collapses, the region risks sliding back into full-scale fighting with civilians on both sides paying first.

Watch Vance's public remarks with Netanyahu and any announcements on aid or next-phase talks in the coming days.

items.title: Four arrested over the Louvre crown-jewels heist as Paris hunts the missing pieces
items.summary:
French police have arrested four more people in connection with Sunday's audacious daytime heist at the Louvre, in which thieves used a crane-mounted furniture lift to reach a gallery window and escaped with historic crown jewels. Prosecutors say the crew was in and out in minutes, dropping a crown belonging to Empress Eugénie as they fled.

Investigators are working from surveillance video, forensic traces and the lift itself, which was reported stolen days earlier. Most of the stolen pieces — including tiaras and necklaces tied to 19th-century French royalty — have not been recovered, and the museum's security practices are under intense scrutiny.

The theft is both a crime story and a cultural one. These jewels are effectively unsellable in recognizable form, which raises fears they could be broken up, and it has forced a national reckoning over how France protects its most visited museum.

Watch for court appearances by the arrested suspects and any word that pieces have been recovered intact.

items.title: Europe weighs a huge loan for Ukraine backed by frozen Russian assets
items.summary:
European Union leaders are weighing how to turn roughly 140 billion euros in frozen Russian central-bank assets into a loan that keeps Ukraine funded. Belgium, where most of the assets sit at the Euroclear clearing house, is demanding shared legal protection before it agrees.

The legal design is delicate: Europe wants to use the assets without formally confiscating them, which officials hope reduces the risk of Russian retaliation and court defeats. Other governments are split between urgency for Kyiv and worry about what the precedent does to Europe as a safe place to park reserves.

Ukraine's budget and war effort depend heavily on decisions like this one. A workable loan would give Kyiv predictable funding into next year; a failure would push the burden back onto national treasuries already under strain.

Watch the summit language this week — whether leaders give the European Commission a firm mandate will signal if this is real or still theoretical.

items.title: Japan gets its first female prime minister as Sanae Takaichi takes office
items.summary:
Japan's parliament elected Sanae Takaichi as prime minister on Tuesday, making the conservative lawmaker the country's first woman to hold the job. She takes over a ruling party weakened by election losses and a sluggish economy.

Takaichi, a longtime ally of the late Shinzo Abe, favors stronger defense spending and a firm line on China, paired with measures to ease household costs. Her early cabinet picks and first Diet battles will test whether she can hold together a fragile coalition.

The appointment is historic for a country that ranks low among democracies on women's representation in politics. It also matters abroad: Japan is a central U.S. ally in Asia, and her government's direction affects trade, technology and regional security.

Watch her first policy speech and how markets and Washington react to her economic team.

items.title: Canada's Carney says the old U.S. trade relationship is over as new tariffs bite
items.summary:
Prime Minister Mark Carney said Canada's once deeply intertwined trade relationship with the United States is over, as new U.S. tariffs on Canadian steel and aluminum took effect this week. Ottawa is accelerating talks with European and Asian partners to diversify where Canadian goods go.

Canadian exporters are already rerouting shipments, and business groups warn of higher costs on both sides of the border. Carney's government is pairing the tougher rhetoric with support for affected industries and a push to remove trade barriers between Canadian provinces.

For Ohio, this is not abstract — Canada is one of the state's biggest trading partners, and supply chains for autos and manufacturing cross the border repeatedly. A lasting rupture would show up in prices and plant decisions across the Great Lakes.

Watch for retaliatory steps from Ottawa and whether Washington offers carve-outs for key industries.

items.title: Shutdown hits Day 22 as a funding vote fails again and Thanksgiving travel worries grow
items.summary:
The federal government shutdown entered its 22nd day on Wednesday after a stopgap funding measure failed again in the Senate, leaving it among the longest shutdowns in U.S. history. Hundreds of thousands of federal workers remain furloughed or working without pay.

The fight centers on health-care subsidies and spending levels, with leaders in both parties publicly blaming the other and privately hunting for an exit. Air traffic controllers and TSA staff calling out sick has begun to snarl some airports, raising fears about Thanksgiving travel if the impasse drags on.

Shutdowns get more expensive the longer they run — delayed paychecks ripple into local economies, food assistance and federal services get shakier, and each failed vote hardens positions.

Watch for any shift in vote counts, or talk of a narrower deal that funds parts of the government first.

items.title: Demolition begins on the White House East Wing for Trump's ballroom project
items.summary:
Demolition crews have begun tearing down part of the White House East Wing to make way for the large ballroom President Trump has long wanted. Preservation groups have asked for a pause and a fuller review, arguing the work is moving before the usual public process is complete.

The administration says the project is privately funded, will respect the building's history, and is needed because state dinners and large events have outgrown existing rooms, often spilling into tents on the lawn. Renderings show a grand hall in a classical style attached to the main building.

The East Wing, built in its current form in the 1940s and home to the first lady's offices, is itself part of White House history — which is why the speed of demolition, not just the design, has become the controversy.

Watch for court or preservation-board action, and whether the first lady's operation announces a permanent new home.

items.title: Obama heads to Cleveland Saturday to rally Ohio voters, with a stop in Solon on the schedule
items.summary:
Former President Barack Obama is set to rally voters in Cleveland on Saturday as Ohio's fall races enter their final stretch, and — in the detail that will matter most around Solon — a stop in Solon itself is on his schedule the same day. The visit is aimed at turning out Democratic voters in Cuyahoga County.

Ohio Democrats are hoping a high-profile closer lifts down-ballot candidates, while Republicans are countering with their own surrogates and arguing the state's recent elections show a durable Republican lean outside the cities.

National figures don't visit by accident. A Solon stop signals both parties see the eastern suburbs — exactly neighborhoods like ours — as persuadable ground worth fighting for in person.

Expect road and crowd impacts Saturday near the event sites; details on tickets and timing are in the linked story.

items.title: Dick Cheney, laid low by illness, will miss his own foundation gala
items.summary:
Former Vice President Dick Cheney, 85, is seriously ill and will miss a gala for his foundation, his family confirmed, asking for privacy. Cheney has a long history of heart disease, including a transplant in 2012 that gave him more than a decade of additional life.

Cheney served as vice president under George W. Bush from 2001 to 2009 and was one of the most powerful holders of the office in modern history, central to the post-9/11 wars in Afghanistan and Iraq. In recent years he broke sharply with his party's current direction, most visibly when he and his daughter Liz Cheney endorsed Kamala Harris in 2024.

Whatever one's view of his record, Cheney shaped American foreign policy for a generation, and news about his health draws statements from across a political spectrum he often divided.

Watch for family updates and tributes from former colleagues in both parties.

items.title: Indiana Republicans weigh a special session to redraw congressional maps mid-decade
items.summary:
Indiana Republican leaders are weighing a special session to redraw the state's congressional districts in the middle of the decade, a move that could net the party additional House seats before the next election. Some state senators remain publicly undecided, which is where the fight will be won or lost.

Mid-decade redistricting, once rare, has become a national arms race this cycle, with both parties looking for map advantages where they control state government. Opponents in Indiana — including some Republicans — argue voters dislike the tactic and that the current maps are barely a few years old.

Control of the U.S. House is likely to be decided by a handful of seats. Even one or two districts redrawn in a state like Indiana can change the national math, which is why Washington is watching a statehouse debate so closely.

Watch whether the governor commits to calling the session — that announcement would start a fast clock.

items.title: Netflix stock slides after an earnings miss tied to a Brazil tax fight
items.summary:
Netflix shares fell sharply in after-hours trading after the streamer reported third-quarter earnings below Wall Street expectations. The company pointed to a roughly $619 million expense tied to an ongoing tax dispute in Brazil as the main reason profit came in light, even though revenue grew about 17 percent year over year to around $11.5 billion.

Underneath the one-time charge, the business looked steadier: Netflix highlighted engagement, advertising growth and a strong content slate, and kept its full-year outlook broadly intact. Investors, however, tend to punish this stock for any crack in a story priced for near-perfection.

The result matters beyond one ticker. Netflix is the bellwether for streaming's mature phase — growth now has to come from ads, pricing and engagement rather than easy subscriber additions, and this quarter shows how exposed even the winner is to overseas tax and currency fights.

Watch management's update on the Brazil case and any guidance changes when the stock trades Wednesday.

items.title: Kimberly-Clark to close its last Ohio diaper plant, cutting about 200 jobs in Marion
items.summary:
Kimberly-Clark says it will close its Marion, Ohio plant — the company's last diaper manufacturing site in the state — eliminating roughly 200 jobs. The maker of Huggies says production will move to other facilities as it consolidates its North American footprint.

Local officials said they were blindsided and are pressing the company on timelines and support for workers. The plant has operated for decades and is one of Marion's larger industrial employers, so the closure lands hard in a community that has absorbed manufacturing losses before.

It is another data point in a familiar Ohio story: consumer-goods production concentrating in fewer, larger plants, with mid-size Ohio towns competing to keep what they have. State job agencies are expected to offer rapid-response help.

Watch for the exact closure date and whether any buyer or new tenant emerges for the site.

items.title: Verizon names a new CEO and plans a major restructuring
items.summary:
Verizon has named former PayPal chief Dan Schulman as its new CEO and is planning a significant restructuring, betting that a leader from outside telecom can fix slowing growth and heavy competition. Outgoing leadership will stay involved during the transition.

Schulman inherits the largest U.S. wireless customer base but a business squeezed by T-Mobile's momentum, cable companies bundling mobile service, and the enormous cost of networks and spectrum. Early priorities are expected to include cost cuts, customer churn and how aggressively to bundle broadband and wireless.

For customers, CEO changes at carriers usually show up first as new promotions, plan reshuffles and store and service changes — worth watching if Verizon is your carrier or internet provider.

Watch for Schulman's first earnings call and any announced layoff or reorganization details.

items.title: Tesla recalls more than 63,000 Cybertrucks over parking lights that are too bright
items.summary:
Tesla is recalling 63,619 Cybertrucks from the 2024 through 2026 model years because a software error can make the front parking lights brighter than federal standards allow, which regulators say could distract other drivers. The fix is a free over-the-air software update — no shop visit required.

It is the latest in a string of Cybertruck recalls covering everything from trim pieces to accelerator pedals, most of them resolved the same way, by pushing new software to the vehicle overnight. Tesla says it is not aware of crashes tied to the lighting issue.

Software-defined cars cut both ways: defects that once meant a dealer trip can now be patched in a driveway, but the recall count also shows how much critical hardware behavior now depends on code.

Owners should get notification letters; if you have a Cybertruck, make sure automatic updates are on.

items.title: The AI data-center boom runs into its limits: power, water and local pushback
items.summary:
The race to build AI data centers is colliding with physical reality. Utilities are warning that power demand from new facilities could strain grids, communities are pushing back over water use and electricity prices, and some projects are being delayed or redesigned.

Ohio is squarely in this story — cheap land, fiber and power have made the state, especially around Columbus, one of the country's data-center hubs. State regulators are now debating who pays for the grid upgrades these giant customers require: the tech companies, or everyone else's electric bills.

That cost question is the one to watch locally. How Ohio answers it will shape both the state's tech economy and household utility rates for years.

Watch the PUCO proceedings and county-level zoning fights, where the boom is being decided project by project.

items.title: Larry Ellison's fortune swells past $350 billion on Oracle's AI run
items.summary:
Oracle co-founder Larry Ellison's net worth has climbed past $350 billion, powered by his roughly 40 percent stake in a company whose stock has surged on massive AI cloud deals. The 81-year-old is now firmly in the conversation for the world's richest person.

Oracle, long known for databases, has repositioned itself as essential infrastructure for AI companies that need enormous computing capacity, signing contracts worth hundreds of billions. Ellison's expanding footprint also includes a major stake in the Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery orbit through his son David's media deals.

Concentrated tech wealth at this scale increasingly shapes media, politics and philanthropy, not just markets — which is why a database fortune becoming an AI fortune is a broader story than a rich list.

Watch Oracle's next earnings for whether the AI backlog converts into delivered data centers on schedule.

items.title: Trump confirms the Louvre heist was raised on his call with Macron
items.summary:
President Trump confirmed he discussed the Louvre crown-jewels heist with French President Emmanuel Macron, calling the theft a terrible thing and saying U.S. officials offered assistance. The topic made an unusual addition to a call otherwise focused on trade and Ukraine.

The comment came as French police made further arrests in the case (see our World coverage). American museum officials are quietly reviewing their own security in response, particularly around smash-and-grab risks.

It is a small moment that shows how a spectacular crime becomes diplomatic small talk — and how security at the world's great museums is now a shared international worry.

No U.S. role in the investigation has been announced beyond the offer of help.

items.title: ICE plans an enforcement operation in Maine focused on Somali immigrants, officials say
items.summary:
Immigration and Customs Enforcement is planning an enforcement operation in Maine focused on the state's Somali immigrant community, according to local officials who say they were briefed this week. Maine is home to one of the larger Somali communities in the U.S., centered in Lewiston and Portland.

City leaders and immigrant advocates say fear is already spreading, with families keeping children home and avoiding public services. Federal officials have not publicly detailed the operation's scope or timing, which is typical before such actions.

Maine's experience will be watched as a test of how far the administration's enforcement push extends into smaller, tight-knit immigrant communities — and how local governments respond when they get advance word.

Watch for statements from Maine's governor and congressional delegation, and any court filings seeking to limit the operation.

items.title: Brazil's Supreme Court upholds Bolsonaro's 27-year sentence as a final appeal is prepared
items.summary:
A panel of Brazil's Supreme Court has upheld former President Jair Bolsonaro's conviction and 27-year prison sentence for attempting a coup after his 2022 election loss. His lawyers are preparing a final appeal, which legal experts say faces long odds.

Bolsonaro was convicted of leading a plot to overturn the election, including plans discussed around the January 8, 2023 riot in Brasília, when supporters stormed government buildings in scenes often compared to January 6 in Washington. He has denied wrongdoing and remains under house arrest while appeals proceed.

The case is a landmark for democracies wrestling with leaders who refuse electoral defeat. Brazil's institutions moved faster and further than many expected, and the ruling cements that outcome barring a surprise reversal.

Watch the final appeal filing and whether Bolsonaro's political movement consolidates behind a successor.

items.title: Magnitude 5.0 earthquake strikes south of Sand Point, Alaska — no damage reported
items.summary:
A magnitude 5.0 earthquake struck about 81 kilometers south of Sand Point, Alaska, on Tuesday, October 20, at a depth of roughly 35 kilometers, according to the U.S. Geological Survey. Sand Point is a small fishing community on Popof Island in the Aleutian chain.

The shaking was rated weak in the few public felt reports filed, and there were no immediate reports of damage in the sources monitoring the event. The Alaska Peninsula and Aleutians are one of the most seismically active zones in the United States, sitting atop the boundary where the Pacific plate dives beneath North America.

Quakes of this size are routine in the chain, but each one is a live test of the monitoring and warning systems that protect Pacific coastal communities from the much larger quakes the region can produce.

USGS may revise the magnitude slightly as more station data arrives; smaller aftershocks are possible.

items.title: Carnegie Mellon lands a blockbuster Mellon Foundation grant for the humanities
items.summary:
Carnegie Mellon University has received a major grant from the Andrew W. Mellon Foundation to expand its humanities programs — a notable bet on literature, history and philosophy at a school best known for computer science and robotics.

University officials say the funding will support faculty, graduate students and public-facing programs connecting the humanities to technology questions — ethics of AI, the history of science and how societies absorb rapid change.

At a moment when humanities funding is shrinking at many universities, a large, deliberate investment at a tech powerhouse sends a signal about what skills the AI era actually needs.

Watch for new centers, fellowships and course offerings announced over the next academic year.

items.title: World Series is set: Rays vs. Brewers, Game 1 Friday
items.summary:
The World Series matchup is set after Tampa Bay closed out the Guardians in the ALCS and Milwaukee finished off its National League opponent: Rays vs. Brewers, with Game 1 on Friday. Neither franchise has a long championship pedigree, guaranteeing a fresh story either way.

For Cleveland fans, the sting is specific — the Guardians' run ended Monday in St. Petersburg, and the Rays team that beat them now plays for a title. Milwaukee, meanwhile, rides a powerhouse season into the Series.

A small-market World Series is also a business story: both clubs win with player development rather than payroll, which front offices everywhere — including Cleveland's — study closely.

First pitch Friday night; expect the Guardians' offseason questions to start in earnest once the Series ends.

items.title: Cleveland's streetcar era is getting a museum-grade second look
items.summary:
A new exhibit and history project is revisiting Cleveland's streetcar era, when electric trolleys stitched together the city's neighborhoods and suburbs — including lines that shaped how the east side developed. Organizers have assembled photographs, maps and restored memorabilia tracing the system from its 1880s peak to its final runs in the 1950s.

At its height, Cleveland's streetcar network was among the largest in America, and its routes still show in the city's bones: wide commercial avenues, streetcar suburbs and the rights-of-way some bus lines still follow today.

For a region debating transit investment now, the exhibit doubles as an argument about what Cleveland once built — and chose to dismantle.

Details on hours and location are in the linked story; history buffs and transit nerds alike will want the map room.

items.title: Mama Santa's, Little Italy's beloved pizzeria, marks a milestone amid a family transition
items.summary:
Mama Santa's, the cash-register-and-red-sauce institution on Mayfield Road in Little Italy, is marking a milestone anniversary this month even as the family behind it navigates a generational transition. Regulars have been stopping in to share memories of first dates, family dinners and post-game slices.

The restaurant has been a neighborhood anchor since the 1960s, famous for its pizza, its prices and a dining room that has resisted every trend Cleveland dining has thrown at it. Family members say the recipes and the room aren't changing.

In a year when Cleveland keeps losing old-school spots, a Little Italy landmark choosing continuity is news worth savoring — literally, if you go.

If you visit this weekend, expect a wait; anniversary crowds plus Little Italy's fall foot traffic are a potent combination.

items.title: Nestlé's Solon factory closure: what we know about the timeline and the workers
items.summary:
More detail is emerging on Nestlé's plan to close its Solon factory by the end of 2027 and shift production to South Carolina. The company's large Solon campus — including its research and development operations — is staying, which separates this from a full exit from the city.

City officials say they are focused on the factory workforce: job-placement help, retraining and working with other area employers who are hiring. The production lines affected make frozen meals, a category Nestlé has been consolidating nationally.

For Solon, the stakes are both human and fiscal — hundreds of households, plus a hit to the income-tax base that funds city services. The long runway to 2027 gives the city time, but not certainty.

Watch for a formal WARN filing, which will put exact job numbers and dates on the record.

items.title: Obama's Saturday Cleveland rally — and Solon stop — puts the eastern suburbs center stage
items.summary:
Barack Obama's Saturday visit leads our local list as well as the national one because of where he's going: a Cleveland rally, plus a scheduled stop in Solon. Campaigns send their biggest closer to the voters they most need, and this year that map runs straight through Cuyahoga County's eastern suburbs.

Local organizers expect large crowds and are urging attendees to arrive early and use transit where possible. Republicans have their own weekend events planned, arguing Ohio's fundamentals favor them.

For Solon residents, the practical news is traffic and crowds Saturday — and the novelty of a former president campaigning in our backyard.

Check the linked Axios Cleveland rundown for venue and timing details before heading out.

items.title: Rock Hall induction week brings a Cleveland music-history spotlight downtown
items.summary:
Rock & Roll Hall of Fame induction festivities are putting downtown Cleveland in a music-history mood this week, with related exhibits, concerts and visitors filling hotels and restaurants around the museum. This year's class and the surrounding programming lean into the Hall's mission of pairing legacy acts with new audiences.

Even in years when the ceremony itself is held elsewhere, the museum anchors a week of events at home — a reminder that the Rock Hall is one of Cleveland's most reliable tourism engines.

If you're heading downtown, expect heavier traffic and fuller restaurants near the lakefront through the weekend.

The linked Signal Cleveland piece rounds up the public events worth your time.

items.title: Overnight fire damages a Tremont apartment building; no serious injuries reported
items.summary:
Cleveland firefighters battled an overnight fire in a Tremont apartment building that displaced several residents but caused no serious injuries, officials said. Crews arrived to heavy fire on an upper floor and kept the blaze from spreading to neighboring buildings on the dense residential street.

The Red Cross is helping displaced residents with temporary housing. The cause is under investigation; officials have not said whether the building's alarms and exits are part of that review.

Tremont's mix of older housing stock and tight streets makes fire response a recurring concern in the neighborhood, and this building's residents now face weeks of displacement.

Watch for the fire marshal's cause determination and any community donation efforts for the families affected.

baby.tip: Hospital-bag week: pack two bags — one for labor and delivery (documents, chargers, snacks for Mike, toiletries, a going-home outfit for Kelly) and one for postpartum and baby (two outfit sizes, since newborn vs 0–3 month fit is a coin toss). Leave them by the door or in the MDX so a midnight departure is grab-and-go. Anything clinical about what to bring for recovery — ask your OB at the next visit.
baby.fact: Newborns arrive with a stomach about the size of a cherry — roughly a teaspoon of milk per feed on day one — which is why tiny, frequent feeds are completely normal at first. By about a week old it has grown to roughly the size of an egg.
